question: What is the meaning of building information modeling (bim) in relation to process?
description: BIM is a collaborative process that integrates various disciplines and stakeholders throughout the building lifecycle. It enables the creation of digital models that contain detailed information about building components, materials, and systems. This information is used to support decision-making, optimize design and construction processes, and improve building performance and sustainability. BIM facilitates communication, coordination, and collaboration among stakeholders, ensuring that everyone has access to the same information and can work together more effectively. The process of BIM involves creating, managing, and updating digital models, which are used to analyze, simulate, and optimize building performance. It also enables the creation of MPs (Material Passports), which contain detailed information about building materials, including their origin, properties, and potential for reuse. This information is crucial for promoting sustainability, reducing waste, and improving the environmental performance of buildings. Overall, BIM is a powerful tool that can transform the construction industry by improving efficiency, reducing costs, and enhancing sustainability.

A study conducted by Atta et al. [2] focused on digitizing MPs using a parametric BIM model to automate sustainability 
metrics for construction projects. This framework was then implemented on a traditional and a modular building alternative, 
with “wet” and “dry” connections. The study highlighted the advances of modular construction, particularly those with dry 
connections, which showed high deconstructability, recovery and environmental performance compared to traditional build­
ing, in addition to the fact that using the parametric BIM model contributes towards semi-automated environmental assessment 
of a building. Likewise, Sanchez et al. [60] introduced a BIM-based Semantic Enrichment Engine for Disassembly Planning 
(SEEDP), which facilitates the efficient retrieval of reusable building components by enhancing MPs with information on 
components’ recovery capacity. This integration is critical for validating the effectiveness of the developed methodology, 
ensuring that it can be feasibly applied to real-world scenarios. Through the case studies, the efficiency and practical application 
of the approach were assessed, and it was shown that the BIM-based MPs methodology is advancing disassembly planning for 
built assets [60]. 
Another study showed that the integration of BIM with circular design principles can foster sustainability in the construction 
industry. Stakeholders can access essential information about building materials by leveraging BIM technology, hence 
improving the communication between various parties and also improving maintenance practices of built assets [1]. Addi­
tionally, it was emphasized that the employment of BIM for creating MPs is crucial due to the fact it ensures that the information 
is structured in a way that is accessible and useful to various stakeholders throughout the building’s lifecycle. Also, initiatives 
such as ORMS MPs policy and “Platform CB’23 ”, which both provided recommendations on the steps and also provided 
detailed data on how to create MPs using BIM at different scales, advocated that implementation of BIM-based MPs at early 
design stages supports material management, sustainability reporting, and regulatory compliance [55,59]. 
Furthermore, in order to address the housing shortage in New Zealand, a BIM-based approach for creating MPs was used to 
enhance data connectivity and automate construction processes [75]. In this study, the methodology involved developing an 
environmental impact calculator to provide key output such as embodied carbon and energy values for materials, through MPs, 
aiding sustainable decision-making during design phases. Additionally, a standardised MP protocol was developed, ensuring 
that comprehensive and detailed data for each construction material was tested through the reuse and categorisation of steel 
components [75].

In the BE, MPs further illustrate how I4.0 technologies can promote CE. MPs are digital documents that contain detailed infor­
mation about building materials, including their origin, properties, and potential for reuse. Blockchain technology ensures that the 
information contained in MPs is secure and tamper-proof, enhancing trust in sustainable building practices. Meanwhile, IoT devices 
embedded in building materials can update MPs with real-time data on the condition of materials, enabling proactive maintenance and 
extending their lifespan. Digital twins further support MPs by allowing construction professionals to simulate how materials can be 
reused in future projects, minimizing waste and promoting resource efficiency.
2.2. Data management and Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) in Building Information Modelling (BIM). How are they related to MPs?
BIM models encompass more than just visual representations; they contain critical information that aids stakeholders in accessing, 
evaluating, and utilizing data effectively with proper management [34]. However, due to the fact that there are many software tools 
could lead to significant compatibility challenges. Efficient collaboration and data interchange between the various stakeholders is 
made possible by open standards like Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) and effective data management procedures [1]. BIM models 
constantly change as a result of contributions from the different stakeholders during the course of the project. Version control is 
ensured by effective data management, allowing teams to monitor changes and operate with the most recent data, improving 
transparency and eliminating mistakes [34]. With this variety of contributors to BIM models, data integrity is essential. In order to 
promote the stakeholders’ confidence in decision-making, rigorous data management protocols are required to provide consistent 
information. This is achieved through the building’s lifespan, as efficiency and sustainability are improved, supported by useful in­
sights through the data-rich environment of BIM [1,34].
For the reasons mentioned above, BuildingSMART created the open IFC standard, which allows easier exchange of building data 
models between the different BIM software platforms and promotes easier cooperation and communication with the various stake­
holders. In contrast to vendor-specific proprietary formats, IFC fosters vendor-neutrality and interoperability, enabling project teams 
to use their favourite tools without sacrificing data integrity [34]. Comprehensive information about 3D geometry, attributes,
